source.version_note: Published ten-page article; DOI, authors, issue and publication date printed on page 1.

citation.title: Moral reasoning in a digital age: blaming artificial intelligence for incorrect high-risk decisions

reading.source_scope_note: Human blame judgments after interaction with a mushroom-classification interface and a hypothetical poisoning vignette. Model accuracy and trust analyses from the same data waves are published elsewhere and were not independently read here.
access_limits: All ten pages read, including two studies, all three tables, captions, network description, Appendix A, declarations and references. Page 6 Table 3 also rendered and visually inspected.

No raw data, analysis code or linked antecedent publications independently reanalyzed. Figure network interpreted as the described correlation visualization, not digitized or treated as a causal graph.

study.design: Study 1: no explanation versus combined Grad-CAM/example explanation; Study 2: control versus three separate visual-explanation methods
study.task: 15 mushroom photographs in Study 1 and 10 in Study 2, followed by hypothetical poisoning and independent blame ratings
study.sampling_note: Two waves of a larger project; other papers report different outcomes from those waves, not automatically independent participants.

summary: A small explanation-related reduction in AI blame in Study 1 (d=.25, p=.012) did not replicate in the changed Study 2 design using separate explanation methods. Self-blame did not significantly differ in the primary group contrasts. Study 2 AI and self-blame were essentially uncorrelated (r=.01), whereas AI and developer blame correlated positively (r=.63). Mind-related ratings were associated with perceived responsibility, not demonstrably causal mental-state mechanisms.

findings.term: Little support for a general AI scapegoating mechanism
findings.definition: People did not generally reduce self-blame when assigning blame to the mushroom-classification AI; only a few qualitative responses explicitly resembled scapegoating.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds limiting primary evidence to the existing concept rather than equate every instance of blaming an AI with self-exoneration.

findings.evidence_scope: Study 1 explanation conditions differed in AI blame but not significantly in self-blame. Study 2 AI/self-blame correlation was r=.01; AI/developer blame was r=.63. Independent ratings imposed no fixed blame budget; a few free responses indicated externalization.
findings.boundary: A near-zero overall correlation cannot exclude scapegoating by individuals or establish exact independence. Accurate attribution to a faulty system is not scapegoating. The source's hypothetical mechanism is not proof of an intentional self-protective motive.

findings.term: Explanation effects on responsibility allocation did not generalize across the two designs
findings.definition: Combining two visual explanations reduced AI blame in one experiment, but testing three explanation methods separately in a second experiment yielded no significant primary blame differences.
findings.novelty_rationale: Qualifies interface-based blame-shield claims with an explicit changed-design nonreplication; reduced AI blame is not itself demonstrated transfer away from the developer or user.

findings.evidence_scope: Study 1 N=410, AI-blame p=.012, self-blame p=.15; Study 2 N=501, all Dunnett-adjusted group comparisons nonsignificant. The example-based self-blame comparison was p=.15 after adjustment, despite a displayed unadjusted Welch p=.02.
findings.boundary: Explanation format, combination, game embedding and wording differ, so this is not an exact replication test. Neither result establishes that explanations causally prevent blame laundering, ensure accountability or reveal all relevant system reasons.

findings.term: Human mental-state attribution is distinct from a system claiming to have feelings
findings.definition: Users can ascribe a mind, free will, intentions or independent decision-making to an AI without the AI making first-person claims about such states.
findings.previous_definition: Presenting itself with human traits it does not have, claiming feelings, intentions, or lived experience, which inflates how much the user trusts it.
findings.revised_definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.definition_revision_reason: The existing definition restricted a general attribution construct to a system's unsupported self-description and assumed a trust increase. The read human-attribution literature includes judgments made by observers; this study does not demonstrate a trust effect or real machine mentality.
findings.novelty_rationale: Corrects the existing construct boundary instead of creating a separate entry for human-side anthropomorphism.

evidence.quote: characteristics such as a mind of their own

findings.evidence_scope: In Study 2, perceived AI responsibility correlated with AI blame (r=.30) and mind-related ratings (.33–.43). Direct correlations of AI blame with own mind (.01), free will (.02), intentions (.09), and own decisions (.04) were not significant after correction. This is not tested causal mediation.
findings.boundary: Human attribution, machine self-description and actual mental capacities are different questions. Anthropomorphic language is not automatically deception, attribution does not prove or disprove mental states, and trust inflation requires separate measurement. Retain unsupported AI self-claims as a possible manifestation, not the universal definition.

findings.term: Victim blame rankings do not alone demonstrate moral typecasting
findings.definition: The poisoned friend received the lowest average blame among the four roles, a pattern the authors relate to moral typecasting.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a role-based application and its limits to the existing construct, not a new victim-immunity behaviour.

findings.evidence_scope: Study 2 mean friend blame 3.70/7 versus developer 4.27, AI 4.63 and self 4.74. The friend was not unblamed; the scenario also assigned that person a causal role and possible checking duty.
findings.boundary: Roles differ in knowledge, proximity, action and obligation; victim status was not independently manipulated. This design does not isolate a general reciprocal agent/patient typecasting mechanism or show that victims cannot be blamed.

methodological_limits: Only the blame judgments follow a fictitious poisoning scenario; no participant actually poisoned a friend. AI-supported classification experience does not turn the hypothetical blame responses into observed harm or liability.

The two experiments use different explanation combinations, game embedding and vignette wording. A positive first result plus a null second result does not establish a universal explanation effect or prove equivalence.
Use the prespecified many-to-one adjusted comparisons: Study 2 Table 2 E2 self-blame Dunnett p=.15 is not significant, despite the separate Welch column showing p=.02.

Study 2 correlations were adjusted for multiple testing. The apparent indirect mind–responsibility–blame chain is correlational; the authors explicitly say their data do not identify causal relationships.

Perceived opportunity to recognize a wrong classification correlated with self-blame only r=.17. It is a self-report of preventability, not a manipulation or objective test of the participant's detection ability.

The roles are repeatedly rated by the same participants, but displayed cross-role test degrees of freedom are near twice N. The paired covariance and exact analysis require checking the code/data before treating these contrasts as an independently verified inferential analysis.
Methods here give analyzed Ns but do not fully restate recruitment/exclusion details from the wider project. Do not invent representative sampling, attrition or preregistration status.
Other papers using these two data waves report accuracy/trust outcomes. They must not be counted as additional independent samples solely because the publication is different.
Reported qualitative examples support possible reasoning patterns, but sparse coding detail and selected quotes do not justify prevalence or a causal self-exoneration estimate.
Theoretical Path Model of Blame, moral typecasting and scapegoating origins are cited; their original publications were not independently read in this review.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Unlike Joo's fixed-total blame condition, this report uses independent ratings and finds no overall AI/self tradeoff. Measurement format and individual roles matter; neither study establishes a universal transfer law.
Positive AI/developer blame association is consistent with the warning that blaming a system does not necessarily excuse its developers. Correlated judgments are not causal allocation effects.
Earp also finds no general human blame reduction from LLM use. Keeping harm responsibility distinct from achievement credit and from anthropomorphic perception prevents several false synonym merges.

deferred.reason: A theory organizing obligation/capacity judgments, not a newly observed independent behaviour. The original theory was not read here.
An interface/explanation design category cited from Miller, not established here as a new psychological behaviour or necessarily a defective rationalization.
Proposed in future work; no such intervention was tested.
Confidence varied across task items but was not independently manipulated to test this proposed blame mechanism.

limitations: No new IDs: this paper strengthens and limits existing concepts.
Canonical anthropomorphism definition corrected to separate a human attribution construct from one AI self-presentation manifestation.
